generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, presenting with authority means more than reporting what you found. You are expected to take a position on what your material shows and to defend it, because every field advances by argument. An academic audience will probe your method and your reading of the evidence. Authority comes from knowing your material well enough to say what it does and does not support, and to concede a limit without abandoning your case.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students presenting the same findings to a seminar, then taking questions.

{{learner-a}} has memorised the slides and delivers them fluently. When someone asks why a conclusion should be trusted when it rests on thin evidence, {{learner-a}} repeats an earlier point and moves on. The talk was smooth, but the argument lived only on the slides. Faced with a fair question, {{learner-a}} had nothing to add. This is delivery without authority.

{{learner-b}} presents the same findings and meets the same question directly. {{learner-b}} acknowledges the weak point, explains why the conclusion still holds given other support, and concedes what would need checking before the claim is secure. The room can see the evidence is understood, not just the slides. This is authority: the case is owned, and it holds up when pushed.

Both students presented the same findings. Only {{learner-b}} could defend them, and that is what an audience reads as authority.
generatedProse.summary: Presenting with authority in any subject means owning your evidence and defending your interpretation, not reciting what you found. You can now explain what authority looks like, recognise it in how a presenter handles a probing question, and choose an authoritative response yourself. The next lesson turns from the individual to the team, and the skills that working together asks of you.

check.body: In the worked example, what gave {{learner-b}} the authority that {{learner-a}} lacked?

items.text: {{learner-b}} answered the challenge directly, conceded the weak point, and defended the conclusion with reasons.
{{learner-b}} delivered the slides more smoothly than {{learner-a}} did.
{{learner-b}} spoke for longer and included more detail.
{{learner-b}} avoided the difficult question to stay on script.

feedback.correct: That's right. {{learner-b}} owned the evidence and defended the interpretation when it was challenged.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} did with the hard question, not how the slides were delivered.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} had authority because the challenge was met, the weak point conceded, and the conclusion defended with reasons. Delivery and length were not the difference.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
